results.title: AI Hardware: CPU vs GPU vs NPU
results.content: # AI Hardware: CPU vs GPU vs NPU. The NPU is a 'super specialist' chip designed specifically for machine learning and AI workloads. Modern CPUs have multiple cores (up to 24 in high-end chips like Intel Core i9-13900KS) for some parallel processing capabilities. However, there are even more parallel chips like Intel's 56-core Xeon W9-3495 processor for data centers. * Deep-learning AI model training (large matrix multiplications). The massive parallelism of GPU architectures with thousands of cores allows them to perform computations much faster than CPUs for workloads that can be parallelized, like graphics rendering and deep learning. However, GPUs are not a total replacement for CPUs. A single CPU core is still far faster than an individual GPU core for serial computational work involving complex branching logic that cannot be easily parallelized or vectorized. GPUs are more like racing cars - high-performance specialized machines optimized for pushing parallel computational throughput to the limits for graphics, AI/ML, etc. Can I use regular CPUs for AI tasks? While CPUs can perform AI tasks, they are generally slower and less efficient than specialized AI hardware like GPUs and TPUs for large-scale or complex AI workloads. NPU is a specialized AI accelerator chip that provides high performance, high efficiency, and low latency for deploying neural networks and machine learning inference at the edge or on mobile devices. * Dedicated Hardware for AI/ML. Like GPUs, NPUs leverage massive parallelism with thousands of tiny processor cores designed to simultaneously perform the many parallel calculations involved in neural network computations. NPUs are engineered to perform AI calculations extremely power-efficiently, allowing AI acceleration in mobile/embedded devices with limited battery/thermal constraints. Major AI/ML frameworks and models like TensorFlow, PyTorch, Caffe, etc., are optimized to run on NPU hardware from vendors like Google, Qualcomm, Intel, etc. ### Learn AI Together. results.title: Real-time ML Inference: Serving Models with Low Latency | by Prathamesh Devadiga | Medium
results.content: # Real-time ML Inference: Serving Models with Low Latency. This isn’t just “smart” software; it’s the result of massive machine learning models working in **real-time**. While training these giant models gets all the headlines, it’s the **inference**, the process of using a trained model to make a prediction, where the real value is delivered to users. Serving a multi-billion parameter model isn’t like querying a database; it’s a massive computational task. It’s not one single trick, but a cascade of optimizations, from rewriting the model’s DNA to using a hyper-specialized serving engine. If you ask a model to translate “hello,” latency is the time you wait until you get “hola” back. The most effective way to increase throughput is to process many requests together in a single batch, as this lets the hardware (especially GPUs) operate at peak efficiency. **Quantization** is the process of converting the model’s weights and activations from `FP32` to a lower-precision format, like 16-bit floats (`FP16`) or, even better, 8-bit integers (`INT8`). In doing so, the student learns the “soft” logic of the teacher model, achieving much higher accuracy than if it were trained on the data alone. A **model compiler** like **NVIDIA’s TensorRT** or **ONNX Runtime** acts like an optimizing compiler for C++. The output is not a general model anymore, but a highly optimized “inference engine” designed for one purpose: to run as fast as possible on a specific target device. Once you have an optimized model, you need a high-performance system to run it. When the window closes, it batches whatever requests have arrived and sends them to the model. To handle challenges like dynamic batching, concurrency, and multi-model serving, we use specialized software. These aren’t web frameworks; they are high-performance C++ applications built for one thing: serving models. * **CPU:** For very small models or applications where every microsecond of latency counts and you can’t afford the overhead of sending data to a GPU.
